title: How Mars landers slow down to land

explain.say: Landing on Mars is hard: the thin air is too thick to ignore but too thin to slow you down by itself. A lander arrives at about 20,000 kilometres per hour and must stop in about seven minutes.

faq.q: Why can't a Mars lander just use parachutes?
faq.a: Mars's air is less than one hundredth as thick as Earth's, so even a giant parachute only slows a lander to a few hundred kilometres per hour. Rockets, airbags or a sky crane must do the rest.
asks: Why is landing on Mars so hard?

faq.a: A rocket-powered descent stage that hovers above the ground and lowers the rover on nylon cables. When the wheels touch, the cables are cut and the sky crane flies off to crash a safe distance away.
Retro-rockets are engines that fire in the direction a craft is moving, pushing against its motion to slow it down. On Mars they fire towards the ground to slow the final descent.
asks: How do rockets slow a lander down?

faq.q: How does a parachute open faster than sound?
faq.a: Mars parachutes are specially designed and tested to survive opening at about 1.7 times the speed of sound, which jerks the craft with huge force. Perseverance's parachute was 21.5 metres across.
asks: How big was the Mars parachute?

faq.q: What are the seven minutes of terror?
faq.a: It is the nickname for a Mars landing. Radio signals take several minutes to reach Earth, so the lander must land entirely by itself, and by the time engineers hear it has started, it has already landed or crashed.
asks: Why can't engineers control a Mars landing live?

facts: Perseverance entered Mars's atmosphere at about 19,500 kilometres per hour and landed in February 2021.
Mars's surface air pressure is less than 1 percent of Earth's.

quiz.why: In such thin air a parachute only gets the speed down to a few hundred kilometres per hour, so rockets finish the job.

wrong.1: Mars has thin air, so parachutes do help, just not enough.
